posts.title: The part you don’t always see
posts.excerpt: To be seen, or not to be seen? There’s something slightly ridiculous about wanting to be Instagram famous but not seen.
posts.body:
One of the questions I get asked quite a lot is, “Where are your video tutorials, blogs and behind-the-scenes videos? We want to see you making things: the mistakes, the process, all of it.”

And honestly... it’s something I’ve battled with for a long time.

There’s a vulnerability that comes with putting yourself, not just your work, out there. And I’m not always very good at it.

I think part of that comes from wanting things to look... well, fabulous. Finished. Considered. Pretty. I love beautiful imagery, beautiful objects and the feeling of presenting something that looks effortless.

The reality of making it, however, is anything but effortless.

Ceramics is messy. It’s dirty. It’s dusty. There’s clay under your fingernails, on your clothes, in your hair and somehow in places you didn’t know clay could possibly reach. There are collapsed forms, cracked pieces, failed firings, wonky pots, experiments that go nowhere and, occasionally, things that I simply think look ugly.

And I think that’s probably something I need to get better at showing too.

Not everything I make is beautiful.

Some things are awkward. Some are clumsy. Some are just plain wrong. Sometimes I pull something from the kiln and immediately think, “Nope. Absolutely not.”

But those pieces are part of the process too. They’re part of learning, experimenting, pushing an idea further and sometimes discovering what not to do next time.

I think another part of it is confidence. I know I make work that I love. I’m proud of what comes out of the studio. But put a camera in front of me and suddenly I’m questioning everything.

Does anyone actually want to see me talking about this?

Do people want to watch me make a mess?

Do they want to see the things that don’t work, or even the things I think just look bloody awful?

And then there’s the slightly embarrassing fact that I don’t particularly like hearing my own voice back.

There’s something slightly ridiculous about wanting to be Instagram famous but not seen. I’m not entirely sure those two things can coexist.

So, I’ve decided it’s something I need to work on.

Over the next few months, I want to change that pattern. To show a little more of the person behind the work. To share more of the process: the good bits, the mistakes, the failures, the experiments, the mess, the things I love and maybe even some of the things I think are ugly. Not that I make ugly work, but some pieces need to be back in the recycling bucket.

Because perhaps that’s actually the part people want to see. The reality behind the finished piece. It feels uncomfortable already. And honestly, it might be one of my biggest challenges yet.

I’d probably find it easier to throw 100 cups blindfolded.

So... wish me luck.

I’m going to try showing my face a little more.

And if you see me awkwardly talking to a camera in the studio, just know that somewhere underneath the nerves is a ceramicist trying very hard to step outside his comfort zone.

posts.title: Make it or break it
posts.excerpt: A collaborative process: a collection of cups for a bespoke store in Melbourne, and the waiting that follows.
posts.body:
Custom orders are always a collaborative effort.

There is, of course, the making: the clay, the wheel, the studio, the hours spent shaping and refining each piece. But there is also a significant part of the process that happens long before the clay is touched. I spend a lot of time with potential clients developing ideas and designing pieces specifically for their spaces, whether that is a private residence, a brand, a small business, or a larger installation.

It begins with conversations. What is the space? How will the pieces be used? What feeling should they bring to it? From those initial discussions, ideas begin to take shape through sketches, proportions, clay and glaze selections, samples and trials. This applies whether I am developing a lighting installation or an entirely bespoke tableware collection. Every detail is considered, tested and refined before the finished work ever reaches its new home.

Recently, I have been working on a collection of cups for a bespoke store in Melbourne. The design is one I have made before, but these versions have evolved: more refined, with slightly different proportions and a new relationship between the components.

The cups combine wheel-thrown vessels with slab-built, hand-cut handles. I particularly like the contrast between the two techniques: the soft curves and subtle throwing lines of the wheel work against the sharper, more linear qualities of the hand-cut slabs. There is something satisfying about bringing those two very different surfaces and processes together to create a single object.

Wheel throwing allows for a certain amount of intuition. You can respond to the clay as it moves beneath your hands, making small adjustments as you go. The slab work is less forgiving. Once the clay is rolled and cut, precision becomes much more important. Measurements matter. Angles matter. Consistency matters.

Measure 100 times, cut once.

Once all the individual pieces are assembled, they become these little statement pieces: considered, tactile and quietly distinctive.

And then comes the waiting.

One of the less glamorous parts of ceramics is patiently waiting for everything to dry. Slowly. Evenly. Carefully. Too quickly and there is a risk of cracking or warping. Too much impatience and all that careful work can unravel before it ever reaches the kiln.

It is, admittedly, a test of my patience. But perhaps that is the whole ceramics process. I should know this already after 8 years.

You learn to slow down. To wait. To accept that clay has its own timeline. You can plan, measure, sketch, refine and control as much as possible, but eventually you have to step back and let the material do what it needs to do.

For me, that balance between precision and unpredictability is part of what keeps me coming back to the studio.

posts.title: 100 Bowls, and then some
posts.excerpt: One hundred bowls. One familiar idea. One hundred individual expressions of it.
posts.body:
The bowl is one of the simplest and most enduring forms we have made.

For thousands of years, across cultures and continents, people have shaped clay into vessels to hold, serve, gather, share and eat. Its purpose has remained remarkably constant, even as the way we live has changed.

The idea for 100 Bowls began with this simplicity.

I wanted to explore a form that is almost universally understood, but to look at it through the lens of contemporary everyday life. What does the bowl mean to us now? It might hold breakfast at the beginning of the day, a handful of fruit on the kitchen bench, a shared meal at the centre of the table, or something as simple as a few treasured objects.

Its function is ordinary, but its presence is constant.

Rather than trying to reinvent the bowl, I wanted to spend time with it.

The 100 bowls became an opportunity to explore the subtle differences within a familiar form: its proportions, curves, weight, depth and relationship to the hand. Each piece became a variation on a theme, allowing me to refine the shapes I naturally gravitate towards while discovering new possibilities along the way.

Ninety-nine percent of the bowls were wheel thrown. A small number were handbuilt from reclaimed clay and leftover pieces collected in buckets around the studio: clay that might otherwise have been discarded, given another opportunity to become part of the collection.

Making 100 bowls is a commitment to repetition, but repetition is never quite as predictable as it sounds.

There were hours upon hours at the wheel. Bowls that collapsed halfway through throwing. Forms that looked right one day and wrong the next. Pieces that cracked or broke in the firing after all the work that had gone into making and finishing them. There were moments of frustration, a sore back, late nights and more than a few sleepless nights spent thinking about clay, forms and firings.

Not every piece made it.

And perhaps that is part of the process.

Working in this way forces you to accept that clay has its own voice. You can guide it, refine it and work carefully, but ultimately the material, the kiln and the process have a say in what survives.

As a ceramic designer and maker, I work in small batches of everyday pieces as well as bespoke collections of contemporary, refined forms. This project brought those two sides of my practice together. The bowls needed to belong to a cohesive collection, but I also wanted each one to have a distinct character of its own.

The aim was not simply to make 100 bowls.

It was to make 100 individual interpretations of a form that has already been made countless times before.

I wanted them to feel considered without becoming precious. Contemporary, but still connected to the history of the vessel. Refined in their form and finish, yet retaining the subtle evidence of being made by hand.

Most importantly, they needed to be used.

A bowl only really comes to life when it becomes part of someone’s daily ritual: held in the hands, placed on the table, filled, emptied and washed, then returned to use again the next day.

That, for me, is where the project became most interesting.

The ancient idea of the bowl remains almost unchanged, but its meaning is continually renewed through the lives we bring to it. 100 Bowls became a reflection on that continuity: an old form, made again and again, finding its place in contemporary life.

And after all the hours, the failed firings, the broken pieces, the frustration and the late nights, there is something deeply rewarding about seeing the collection together.

A sense of pride, certainly.

But also a quiet satisfaction in knowing that each bowl began simply as a lump of clay, and through time, touch, patience and fire, became something made to be used and lived with.

One hundred bowls. One familiar idea. One hundred individual expressions of it.
